summary: Defines an SMTP extension for relaying message bodies with text outside the US-ASCII range. It was a draft standard. It was replaced by RFC 6152.

eli5.summary: A way for mail computers to agree they can pass along messages with letters from other languages. A newer version replaced it.

questions: how does smtp send 8 bit text
subtitle: How two mail servers agree to pass message bodies that use 8-bit characters, not just 7-bit ASCII.

tldr.problem: SMTP originally carried only 7-bit US-ASCII text, but many people wanted to exchange MIME messages containing arbitrary octet-aligned material.
tldr.mechanism: The server advertises the 8BITMIME keyword in its EHLO reply, and the client adds a BODY=8BITMIME or BODY=7BIT parameter to the MAIL FROM command.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1652 was a Draft Standard that obsoleted RFC 1426 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 6152.

today: RFC 1652 was a Draft Standard that obsoleted RFC 1426. It has itself been obsoleted by RFC 6152, which is the current specification of the 8BITMIME extension.

sections.title: The Problem and the Limits
sections.content:
SMTP is widely deployed, but a significant part of the Internet community wanted to exchange messages whose body is a MIME message containing arbitrary octet-aligned material. RFC 1652 uses the SMTP service extension mechanism (RFC 1651) to define the 8bit-MIMEtransport extension.

The extension does not remove line-length limits. Servers may still limit lines, but no lower than 1000 octets. So it does not provide a way to transfer unencoded binary data through SMTP.
sections.eli5: Mail used to carry only simple letters. This lets it carry more kinds of letters, but still not raw computer files.

sections.title: The Extension Framework
sections.content: The RFC lists the parts of the extension. Its name is 8bit-MIMEtransport, and the EHLO keyword is 8BITMIME with no parameters. One optional parameter, BODY, is added to the MAIL FROM command. Its value is either 7BIT, meaning a message in strict compliance with RFC 821, or 8BITMIME, meaning a MIME message with arbitrary octet content. No new SMTP verbs are defined.
sections.eli5: The server shows a sign saying '8BITMIME ok'. The sender then says whether this particular letter is plain or fancy.

sections.title: How Client and Server Behave
sections.content:
A client first sends EHLO. If the server answers with code 250 and includes 8BITMIME, it will accept MIME messages with arbitrary octet-aligned content. The client then sends MAIL with a single BODY parameter after the address. A server that supports the extension shall preserve all bits in each octet and must deliver or relay the content so that all bits are preserved.

The usual SMTP data-stuffing rules still apply, so a lone dot line ends the message. Line length is still subject to server limits, which may be as low as 1000 octets.

If the server does not advertise 8BITMIME, the client must not, under any circumstances, send content outside the US-ASCII range (hex 00-7F). It has two options. It can convert the message to valid 7bit MIME, with no loss of information, or it can treat the case as a permanent delivery failure. The RFC does not describe the conversion itself.
sections.eli5: Always ask first. If the other side says no, either rewrite the letter in plain letters or give up and tell the sender.

sections.title: Example and Security
sections.content:
The RFC gives a sample dialogue in which the server advertises 8BITMIME, the client sends MAIL FROM with BODY=8BITMIME and the message goes through.

On security, the RFC does not discuss security issues and says it is not believed to raise any beyond those already present in electronic mail and in fully conforming implementations of RFC 821.
sections.eli5: The example shows the asking and answering step by step. The RFC says this change does not add any new safety worries.
